source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
source.authors: Hoagy Cunningham; Aidan Ewart; L. Smith; R. Huben; Lee Sharkey

record.tranche_reason: The study compares automated interpretability measurements of MLP neurons and learned features, and examines how the measured score changes with scoring and activation-range choices. It does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The indirect-object-identification patching results compare feature decompositions on task localization, not neuron polysemanticity, so they are not rows. Reconstruction perplexity and hyperparameter sweeps likewise do not directly measure the claim. Scores and curves shown only in figures are not transcribed as numeric values.
record.test_reason: The paper takes neuron polysemanticity and superposition as motivation. Its results score its own sparse-autoencoder features against baselines (neurons, PCA, ICA, random directions). Neuron interpretability appears only as a comparison baseline, shown in figures. No prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons, cause, or architecture dependence is measured. So it relies on the finding and reports its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised way to take language-model features out of superposition. They say the learned features are more interpretable (by autointerpretation) and more monosemantic than neurons, PCA, ICA and random directions. The features also localise IOI behaviour more finely. Limitations are imperfect reconstruction (layer-2 perplexity rises from 25 to 40), mixed success on MLPs with many dead features, and limits of automated interpretation. Gains shrink in later layers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders and automated feature-interpretability scoring rather than the original neuron-visualization approach; the study also compares feature decompositions and performs activation patching.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability scores vary with top-and-random versus random-only scoring and by layer; the authors report reduced gains in later layers. MLP feature learning is mixed and can yield many dead features.

fits_no_version.finding: A residual-stream basis dimension is dominated by apostrophes in its upper activation range. Those apostrophes explain little of the middle-to-lower ranges, so the authors call it polysemantic. They also state that residual basis directions are no more interpretable than random directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-stream basis dimensions in transformers are polysemantic, and their apparent meaning depends on the activation range examined.

record.problems: The central interpretability measure is automated and the authors discuss limitations of automatic interpretation. The MLP analysis has mixed success and many dead features. Several relevant results are presented in figures without numeric values in the text; the study does not quantify neuron polysemanticity prevalence.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for task-patching comparisons or reconstruction perplexity: these measure feature localization or reconstruction effects rather than neuron polysemanticity or measurement dependence.

untested.parts: No count or share of polysemantic MLP neurons, nor layer-wise prevalence; neuron scores serve only as a baseline in figures.
Superposition is assumed as motivation; no test that capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
SoLU and architectural sparsity are only cited in related work; no manipulation of the trained model.
Scoring and activation-range choices are examined only to validate the SAE features, not to test whether neurons' polysemantic status depends on measurement.

missing.what: Top-and-random and random-only autointerpretability scores for MLP neurons by layer. These are the only quantitative neuron-interpretability values that might bear on V2, and they are readable only from the figure.

record.verdict_notes: This is an original SAE methods paper. Polysemanticity is the motivation, not the object of measurement. All quantitative comparisons are SAE features versus baselines, and the key neuron numbers appear only in figures. I reclassified the study from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4 and removed the reader's V2 and V7 labels.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not quantify the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or establish prevalence across transformer language models.
The study motivates sparse feature dictionaries using superposition, but does not establish that capacity pressure causes neurons’ polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Effects of changing a model’s activation function, architecture, or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons, and any associated performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons have one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
The study examines selected activation-range and automated-scoring choices, not all possible measurement methods or explanation scores.

rows.subject: Pythia model used for MLP analysis (exact model not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared automated interpretability scores for MLP dictionary features and neurons across MLP layers.
rows.value: The authors report that the approach finds many features more interpretable than neurons, but also report mixed success and many dead features; numeric scores are shown only in Figure 10.
rows.note: This is a score-based comparison, not a count of neurons activating for unrelated contexts. The text does not state the exact model for this MLP analysis.
rows.check: This compares SAE features (the study's own method) with MLP neurons. It is not a measure of how many neurons respond to unrelated contexts. Neuron scores appear only in Figure 10, and the 'partial' state describes the SAE's mixed success, not neuron polysemanticity. The subject model is unstated.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Recomputed autointerpretability scores using randomly selected fragments only, rather than top-and-random fragments.
rows.value: Random-only scores are reported as significantly smaller; learned features still outperform baselines, especially in early layers. Numeric values are shown only in Figure 9.
rows.note: The authors note that limited random samples may underestimate performance for heavy-tailed features.
rows.check: This is a robustness check that the method's advantage survives random-only scoring. It compares the study's own method against baselines. It does not show that a neuron's polysemantic status flips with the scoring choice. Values are in Figure 9 only.

rows.subject: Pythia residual-stream basis dimension (exact model and layer not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Examined a token-activation histogram across activation ranges for a residual-stream basis dimension.
rows.value: The upper activation range contains many apostrophes, but this accounts for very little variance in the middle-to-lower ranges; the authors describe the dimension as polysemantic.
rows.note: The text identifies this as the residual-stream dimension most associated with the apostrophe feature among the dimensions considered, but does not state its layer or model.
rows.check: A single residual-stream basis dimension, which the authors say has no privileged basis, is not an MLP or vision neuron. It is a qualitative illustration chosen by search, not a measurement of a version. Better recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The authors report that many learned features are more interpretable than MLP neurons, consistent with neuron polysemanticity, though the score does not quantify how many neurons respond to unrelated contexts (r1).
